author: swyx .ai
text: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. text: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. author: swyx .ai
text: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion . What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
author: Basil Chatha
text: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → Open video on YouTube ↗ What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering. Jump to the billing model discussion → Evals without access to customer data Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm. So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags. title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
author: Richard MacManus
text: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system . “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.” In other words, there are certain tools and tasks the agent can execute by itself — but not ones that involve risk to the client. Arca also runs verification checks on known AI security issues, such as prompt injections. Arca’s agent isn’t itself sandboxed, but it does use sandboxes for computation. Singh explained they’ve gone even further, with extra security measures for handling sensitive data. “We've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data,” he said. “So we have this thing which translates the code it [the agent] wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and you install guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data, which means that they can aggregate it, they can munge it, they can work with it as they see fit to produce [things] like a financial plan.” Another interesting process Arca has implemented is using feedback from human advisors, along with traces from the agents, to improve the harness. A “meta-agent” is used to analyze all this data and suggest changes to the harness. title: Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
author: icyfox
text: Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS. I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to run them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started. A few unique design decisions in waymark: — Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic. — Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production. — It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here. — Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove. It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime. What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job. I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

title: Ears Open
author: Alan Page
text: I had a pep talk ready before I got to the tree. In the desert section of the PCT, another hiker and I had been leapfrogging each other for a few days, chatting a bit about life and trail. I turned on a switchback, and she was sitting on the side of the trail, in the shade of a tree with her shoes off and her head down. I knew exactly what I was looking at, because I’d been there myself. Sore feet, too many miles, and sometimes wondering why anyone would do all of this on purpose. So I asked her if she would share her shade, sat down next to her, and talked for a bit about my worst day on the trail, how amazing it was to be out here, and how tomorrow would be better. “Thanks,” she said. “My feet are fine, and I’m having fun. This is the first signal I’ve had in three days, and I’m waiting to hear how my dad’s surgery went.” I’d spent five minutes attempting to comfort her about something that wasn’t happening, and until that moment, I’d been happy with myself for doing the “right” thing. So I stopped talking and asked about her dad. For the next 20 minutes, she told me about him, and somewhere in there I stopped thinking about how I thought she must feel and started feeling it. When her phone finally buzzed, my stomach dropped along with hers. (The surgery was minor, and he was completely fine.) Eyes Open A few years ago, I wrote a post called Eyes Open about what happens after a hard decision. It leaned on a line from Leadership on the Line that I’ve been repeating for most of my career: “Leadership is disappointing people at a level they can absorb.” In that post, I talked about the difference between cognitive empathy, where you take someone else’s perspective, and social empathy. I said cognitive empathy applies more often when you’re dealing with the fallout of a hard decision. I stand by most of that, but I’ve since learned it comes with a catch, because I took my fellow hiker’s perspective as hard as I could and got it completely wrong. The same thing happens at work. When you cancel a project your lead has spent a year on, you’ll probably prepare by imagining what it feels like to watch that work go away. Then she tells you she’s known it was in trouble since June, and that what she’s worried about is the engineer who moved across the country to work on it. Taking Perspective Tal Eyal, Mary Steffel, and Nicholas Epley ran 25 experiments to test whether imagining someone else’s point of view makes you better at knowing what they think and feel. Most of the people they surveyed expected that it would. The researchers couldn’t find consistent evidence that it did, and if anything, people got less accurate overall, even though it sometimes made them more confident. That held up with people who knew each other well, including spouses. The tests were things like reading emotions and predicting preferences rather than a hard conversation with a lead, but I recognize the pattern. I sat down under that tree feeling like I was prepared, and all that preparation had come from inside my own head. The research isn’t an argument against trying. Imagining someone’s situation made people less likely to project their own feelings onto others, and Epley says it may help us care more about them. My pep talk came from a good place. It just couldn’t tell me what my fellow hiker was waiting for. Perspective The last experiment in the paper compared imagining with talking. People who got the other person’s perspective directly, through conversation, became more accurate, and the ones who only imagined it didn’t. The authors’ conclusion is that understanding someone comes from “getting perspective, not simply taking perspective.” That research measured accuracy, and there’s something else I’ve realized that it can’t measure. In Eyes Open , I gave cognitive empathy most of the credit, and I’d give the other kind of empathy a lot more now. Imagining how someone feels gets me to a description of their experience. title: Linky #41: What are we basing our confidence on?
author: Jit Gosai
text: This week’s links got me thinking about one particular topic: confidence. We’re regularly building software with varying degrees of uncertainty and making decisions with incomplete information. We need confidence in the decisions we’re making, but that confidence needs to come from somewhere. So what evidence are we using, and how much can we trust it? This week’s links explore that from a few different angles, from probabilistic thinking and code coverage to agentic evals, AI adoption and the conditions that help people learn. Latest post from the QE Newsletter I’ve been down a bit of an AI rabbit hole recently, thinking about what Quality Engineering could mean in an agentic engineering world, where we’re increasingly using AI agents to build software. One thing that’s become apparent to me is that by developing a better understanding of what could go wrong, we can start thinking about how we influence and respond to systems that behave unpredictably. In some ways, this feels a little more manageable, as we have a better understanding of where some of our uncertainty is coming from, and there are ways to guide, constrain, monitor and, to a lesser extent, control agent behaviour. But none of these approaches guarantees the outcomes we want. And I think that’s something we as an industry need to start acknowledging and getting more comfortable with. We’re going to be shipping software with uncertainty , something we’ve always done, but the speed and autonomy that agents introduce could make the consequences much harder to anticipate and manage. Rather than pretending we can eliminate that uncertainty, we need to develop ways of understanding it, making it visible and responding when things don’t go as expected. That’s really what I’ve been exploring in this post. How do teams learn what works, establish appropriate boundaries and develop the confidence to work with agents without simply hoping for the best? Because, as a friend recently reminded me, hope is not a strategy. Thinking in probabilities I was watching this video on 20 years of productivity advice , and one of the habits described was thinking in probabilities. Which got me thinking that this is something we have to do a lot as QEs. We’re working in complex systems where knowing every possible outcome is impossible. You’re almost constantly hedging your bets that things will work, but there’s always a situation or circumstance you’ve not considered. So thinking in probabilities doesn’t just keep us open to more information. It also helps stop us from looking only for evidence that confirms what we already believe and holding on too tightly to our beliefs when new evidence emerges. One mistake I made was thinking it’s just about percentages and fractions, e.g. ‘I’m 80% confident that this will work’. While that can help, it’s also about thinking in degrees of confidence. Such as ‘I might be missing something here’, and separating the decision from the outcome. For instance, you might make a good decision based on the evidence available, but the outcome could still be wrong because of something outside your control. Which makes me wonder how often we judge the quality of our decisions based on what happened afterwards, rather than what we knew at the time. title: Agentic engineering: The controls aren't enough
author: Jit Gosai
text: A few weeks ago, I heard Maryna Didkovska share a story about an AI agent handling customer refunds . Anything over $500 was supposed to require human approval, but the agent ended up processing around $1.2 million in refunds over 18 hours. It did its job well, a little too well, and the decisions it made weren’t quite what the organisation intended. And it got me thinking about how we work with agents. Not just how we know they’ve done what we’ve asked, but how we make sure they’re acting within the boundaries we’d intended. Especially when you consider that it’s well documented that agents can claim they have completed things when they haven’t or that they can fail to follow instructions , particularly during complex tasks. So we can’t always predict how they’ll behave, and taking their word for when they say they’re done seems risky. So what do we do? Principles we should adopt Well, two principles I think we should adopt are ones I learned from Dragon Spiridonov : Done as a hypothesis and Evidence over claims . Done as a hypothesis is about how agents and LLMs will report that they’ve finished, but that’s not evidence that it’s actually done what it has said it has done. So we should treat reports of job completion as a hypothesis that we should test. And we need to define these upfront before the work is even started. This way, done becomes a testable claim once the work is complete and can be checked. But this isn’t a panacea, and we need to define clear completion criteria, which can be tricky when we’re exploring new ideas. There is a risk you define the wrong criteria or overlook important behaviours. The second principle is evidence over claims . If an agent reports that it’s done something, then there should be actual evidence that it’s done those things, e.g. execution logs, test results, code diffs, commit hashes, observable system behaviour. This makes its claims traceable and auditable, but these often only tell you the existence of artefacts. They could still be incomplete, misleading or irrelevant. For example, a passing test doesn’t tell you the right thing was tested. Also, collecting large amounts of evidence can create noise and make it harder to see what is relevant. But what happens when an agent actually has done everything it claims? So the evidence supports those claims, but the outcome isn’t something we intended? That’s what interested me about the refund story. It wasn’t necessarily about whether the agent had completed the work. It was about whether it should have been allowed to make all those decisions in the first place. Which then got me thinking about how we actually do this. How do we influence agent behaviour? This is where I went down a bit of a rabbit hole. There are lots of techniques and approaches in this space, and more are emerging. Dragon shared a few in his talk at HUSTEF, such as rules in agent MD files, post-tool-use hooks, pre-flight skills checks, custom MCP lookups, defensive prompting, and real-time per-turn monitoring. There’s also LLM-as-a-judge, and I was at the early preview of Thoughtworks technology radar last week, where they shared even more tools and techniques. With so many options, it feels quite overwhelming: what works, what doesn’t and what makes sense for your context. So I started to pull them all out to see if any patterns emerged in what they do and how they help. And two broad categories stood out. Some approaches try to influence agent behaviour, while others try to detect or constrain their behaviour. To influence behaviours, some tools and techniques try to provide guidance through instructions, rules and checklists. Then, in order to reduce uncertainty, some approaches give context by helping agents access relevant information when making decisions. title: Linky #40: What are we actually trying to achieve?
author: Jit Gosai
text: Whether that’s organisations focusing on predictable outputs rather than outcomes, developers identifying their value with writing code, or experiments becoming production systems. In each case, we start with something useful, but somewhere along the way, the activity can become more important than the reason we started doing it in the first place. And I think this is something we need to be careful of in quality engineering too. It’s easy to become focused on the practices, tools and processes we use, rather than what we’re actually trying to achieve with them. Latest posts from the QE Newsletter I’ve been travelling a lot over the last three weeks, so I’ve got four shorter QEN posts to share. Being heard is not the same as being understood . This gets into the responsibility of both the person sharing and the person hearing, and it comes back to feedback loops. Specifically, checking for understanding and making sure you’re using language the other person understands. Resilience is not about being unbreakable . There are some big changes going on at work at the minute, and I started thinking about resilience. Which reminded me of an idea from resilience engineering about resilience being less about being unbreakable and more about flexing, bending, extending and even breaking to save the wider system. I think a few of these ideas could apply to personal resilience too. I’ve been to three different conferences over the last three weeks, and AI was the dominant topic. But what caught my interest was the QE side of AI and when AI says it’s done, how do we know? . For me, I feel the anthropomorphising of LLMs is the real risk. When we treat these tools as people, we’re more inclined to trust what they say rather than see them for what they are, tools that need to give us evidence that the trust is warranted, not because they said so. Having delivered three different talks on quality engineering at three different conferences, a tension I’ve felt with QEN bubbled up to the surface: I can’t tell you what to do or how to do it . I don’t work in your teams or understand your context. But what I can do is share ideas, research, experiences and practical approaches that might help you better understand what’s going on in your environments and maybe help you create healthier environments that are more conducive to better quality outcomes. text: Cześć! Z tej strony Przemek - w to sobotnie przedpołudnie wracam z kolejnym wydaniem Przeprogramowanego Newslettera i na start kilka słów o tym, jak planujemy nasz jesienno-zimowy kalendarz po ukończonej edycji 10xDevs 4.0. Pierwszym istotnym elementem całej układanki jest inwestycja w podcast Opanuj.AI - chociaż docelowy “obrazek” wciąż przed nami, to już teraz widać zmiany. Widać, bo widzimy się na żywo w studio, a nie po dwóch stronach Streamyarda. Możecie nas oglądać choćby na YouTube , no i od listopada częściej, bo dwa razy w miesiącu. Podcast to miejsce, w którym staramy się narzucać jak najmniej ograniczeń i występować przed wami bez filtra. Listopadowe odcinki pokażą, że nasze nastawienie do AI wcale nie jest tak oczywiste i jednoznaczne, jak mogłoby się wydawać (co zresztą wiedzą już absolwenci 10xDevs). Dowód? Kolejny odcinek będzie o fuckupach w kodzie i kontrargumentach do hipotezy o tym, że w kod nie warto już zaglądać. A co poza podcastem? Nie zabraknie nas na scenie takich wydarzeń jak DevFest Wrocław, na ścieżce AI (13-14 listopada), oraz na InfoShare Katowice (17-18 listopada). Na obu wydarzeniach opowiemy o “Why?” naszego 10xWorkflow, czyli frameworka zapewniajacego bezpieczną i jakościową pracy z agentami AI. Dla absolwentów 10xDevs temat znany jest bardziej, dla reszty społeczności być może nieco mniej, ale na obu wydarzeniach tak czy tak pojawią się smaczki, których do tej pory nie publikowaliśmy w żadnym innym miejscu. No dobra, a jak nie podcast i nie scena, to czy wy panowie w ogóle jeszcze coś budujecie, czy tylko kursiki i prezentacje? Hmm… powiedziałbym, że zabawa dopiero się rozpoczyna. Nasze techniczne laboratorium wzbogaciło się o dwie sztuki całkiem ładnej podstawki na monitor, która przy okazji pozwala nam odpalać całkiem niezłe lokalne modele AI ;) Wnioskami z konfiguracji i pracy na Makach Studio podzielimy się już wkrótce - zainwestowaliśmy w ten hardware bo wierzymy, że otworzy to dla nas zupełnie nowe ścieżki zarówno rozwoju wewnętrznego, jak i tego, co możemy zaoferować naszej społeczności - zarówno zupełnie za free jak i w szkoleniach dedykowanych. No i na koniec jeszcze jeden temat, który również w laboratorium jest już rozpracowywany. Co po 10xDevs 4.0? To proste - najlepsza edukacja o AI (dla ludzi, nie dla agentów) na polskim rynku. Lecimy! 🧑‍💻 Technicznie Komponenty pamięci agenta - Większość zespołów zakłada, że im więcej agent zapisze w notatkach i im dokładniejsze dostanie reguły, tym lepiej pracuje w kolejnych sesjach. Ale czy zawsze? Lance Martin z Anthropic opisuje serię eksperymentów z pamięcią agentów i pokazuje, że najmocniejszym modelom lepiej służy swoboda niż sztywne instrukcje. Dodaje też czym jest śnienie, i dlaczego ten efekt jest kluczowy dla agentów nowej generacji. Github aktualizuje swoją infrastrukturę - Git to dla większości z nas narzędzie, o którym się nie myśli, bo zawsze działa. Tylko co będzie, gdy do jednego repozytorium zaczną wypychać zmiany tysiące agentów naraz? Inżynierowie GitHuba opisują, jak przebudowują przechowywanie repozytoriów z myślą o ruchu, który agenci mają generować przez całą dobę. W wewnętrznych testach nowa architektura przyjmuje 7200 pushy na sekundę do jednego repozytorium, a zespół przyznaje, że kluczowym wyzwaniem jest przyśpieszająca w niesamowitym tempie liczba operacji Read. MCP - animowane i w kolorze - Kiedy podpinasz agentowi serwer MCP, łatwo założyć, że model łączy się z narzędziem bezpośrednio przez kolejne REST API. Tyle że protokół działa inaczej. Interaktywny przewodnik od Runlayer rozkłada go na role i wiadomości, które krążą między aplikacją, modelem i serwerem, a każdy krok prześledzisz na diagramie. Osobna sekcja pozwala też samemu zepsuć ten układ i zobaczyć, gdzie bywa podatny na atak. text: Hej, Marcin z tej strony 👋 Co robisz, gdy Twój przyjaciel i wspólnik ma prelekcję w Katowicach? Przez ostatni rok mogłem mu jedynie wysłać z Poznania wiadomość w stylu „good luck and have fun”. Na szczęście powrót do Krakowa zmienił zasady gry i mogłem kibicować Przemkowi na miejscu, podczas czwartkowego BRAVE AI Community Meetup w Rawa.Ink. Podczas prelekcji Przemek pokazał jak korzystać z 10x-bench-kit , naszej open source’owej biblioteki do porównywania modeli i agentów. Zaczęło się od przekonania, że warto podnieść poziom dyskusji o tym z czego korzystać do programowania z AI ponad znane i lubiane “Opus 5.5 jest INSANE, ma 64.8% w TerminalBench i na X piszą, że AGI” 10x-bench-kit pozwala tworzyć własne rankingi AI poprzez porównywanie jak agenci radzą sobie z realizowaniem zadań w Twoim projekcie. Takie ewaluacje to świetny punkt wyjścia do podejmowania świadomych decyzji - z czego korzystać, za co płacić. A sam proces tworzenia własnego rankingu pozwala głębiej zrozumieć różnice pomiędzy modelami, harnessami i agentami. Przemek otworzył meetup, ale odbyły się jeszcze dwie prezki: Przemysław Barański i Krzysztof Kijas z jaktestowac.pl zaprezentowali framework e2e od TesterArmy (Polska gurom). Fajnie było poznać ten duet na żywo - do tej pory kojarzyliśmy się z internetów i 10xDevs. Dostaliśmy upominek w postaci testersko-metalowych koszulek. Już wiem co założę na kolejny koncert Linkin Park, dzięki 🤘 Na koniec eventu Kuba Ploskonka zaprezentował swoje wszechstronne środowisko developerskie oparte o Kubernetes, w którym wiele agentów pracuje w izolowanych kontenerach. Fajne połączenie inżynierskiego rygoru z elastycznością użycia. Dużo inspiracji na poziomie architektury i konkretnych narzędzi. Dzięki Szymon Łakomy i Miłosz Korbaś za organizację meetupu. Dzięki również wszystkim, z którymi miałem okazję się przywitać i zamienić słowo. Do następnego! 🧑‍💻 Technicznie W czasach AI pracujemy ciężej niż kiedykolwiek - Tanie wytwarzanie kodu zwiększa obciążenie inżynierów - wbrew założeniu, że programistom będzie lżej. Równoległe uruchamianie wielu agentów przesuwa wąskie gardło z pisania kodu na przełączanie kontekstu i weryfikację zmian. Dane z repozytoriów pokazują, że aktywność menedżerów technicznych jest na podobnym poziomie co u szeregowych programistów. Warto rozważyć wprowadzanie limitów równoległych prac badawczo-wdrożeniowych, bez nich organizacjom grozi fala wypalenia zawodowego przez nadmiar asynchronicznych decyzji. Możesz budować systemy, na które wcześniej nie było zasobów - Spadek kosztów generowania kodu zmienia rachunek opłacalności wielu projektów inżynierskich. Zadania uznawane dotąd za stratę czasu, jak pisanie własnych silników bazodanowych, interpreterów czy narzędzi deweloperskich, można dziś z pomocą agentów zrealizować w kilka godzin. Programiści, którzy potrafią weryfikować architekturę i tworzyć własne, niestandardowe narzędzia mają przed sobą świetlaną przyszłość. tsrc: szybszy i lżejszy TypeScript - Cloudflare, VoidZero i Owner.com zaprezentowały tsrs , oficjalny port kompilatora TypeScriptu na Rusta, rozwijany w ramach projektu Oxc. Narzędzie przyspiesza sprawdzanie typów nawet 8-krotnie i zmniejsza zużycie pamięci o 70% w porównaniu z TypeScript 7.0. Rusta wybrano ze względu na wydajność w WebAssembly. text: “Drodzy państwo, z tej strony wasze państwo – wyłączamy usługi publiczne, dopóki PHP nie zostanie załatane.” Ile razy w trakcie ostatniej dekady spotkaliście się z takim komunikatem? I jak zareagowalibyście na niego jeszcze tydzień temu? Science fiction? Żart? Scenariusz filmu Netflixa? No cóż - to właśnie nasza rzeczywistość pod koniec 2026r. Przyznam, że liczba napływających do nas informacji o cyberkryzysie napędzanym przez masowe wykorzystanie AI do atakowania serwisów internetowych naprawdę mnie zaniepokoiła. Jak na dłoni widać, że technologia trafia do mas, a część tych mas nie ma szczególnie przyjaznych intencji wobec reszty świata. Do niedawna przeprowadzenie skutecznego ataku wymagało odpowiednich kompetencji, czasu i niemałych zasobów. Dziś AI pozwala ominąć przynajmniej część tych barier, a skala zjawiska zaczyna wyprzedzać zdolność organizacji do reagowania. Nie trzeba nawet tworzyć genialnego exploita za pierwszym podejściem. Wystarczy wygenerować i przetestować odpowiednio dużo przeciętnych. Zakładam, że skoro czytacie nasz newsletter, nie trzeba Was ewangelizować o potencjale sztucznej inteligencji. Jeśli jednak ktoś wciąż traktuje AI jako technologiczną ciekawostkę, właśnie otrzymał kolejny argument za zmianą perspektywy. Niestety, niekoniecznie taki, na jaki liczyliśmy. No dobra, to co nam zostaje - panikować? Zdecydowanie nie. Paradoksalnie to właśnie chłodna głowa i zdrowy dystans do kolejnych doniesień o kryzysie mogą dać nam przewagę. Zamiast bezradnie obserwować rosnącą skalę zagrożeń, warto potraktować obecną sytuację jako impuls do przeglądu własnych praktyk, infrastruktury i sposobu myślenia o bezpieczeństwie. Reguły gry się zmieniają, więc nasze narzędzia i nawyki również muszą za nimi nadążać.
